Common questions

Things people ask
before they commit.

Do you work to a fixed price or cost-plus?

Both, depending on the project. What doesn't change is that you see the full costing schedule either way — every trade, every allowance and our margin — so you know what sits behind the number you're agreeing to.

How early should we talk to you?

Earlier than most people do. If you bring us in before the design is locked, we can tell you what your site and your council will allow, and which decisions are quietly setting your budget. It costs you nothing and it saves redesign fees later.

Which parts of Adelaide do you build in?

Across metropolitan Adelaide and the Hills — from the coastal suburbs through to Stirling and the surrounding districts. We know the councils, the heritage overlays and the soil.

How many projects do you take on at once?

Deliberately few. It's the only way Jordan can be on every site rather than managing yours from a distance.

A custom home is the only house you'll ever live in that was designed around your mornings.

We build a small number of custom homes each year, on land our clients have usually spent a long time finding. Some come to us with a completed architectural set; others come with a survey, a budget and an idea, and we bring the design team to the table.

Either way, the work starts with the site. Fall, orientation, soil classification, easements, overlays — these set more of your budget than the floor plan does, and knowing them early is what keeps a project honest.

How it runs

to handover.

01

Site and feasibility

We walk the land with you, pull the planning overlays, and give you a realistic cost range before you spend money on documentation. If the numbers don't work, you'll hear it here.

02

Design and documentation

Working with your architect or ours, we cost the design as it develops rather than at the end — so choices are made with the number in view, not against it.

03

The open-book contract

You receive the full costing schedule: every trade, every provisional sum, every supplier quote and our margin. Nothing is folded into a lump you can't interrogate.

04

Construction

A fixed site team, a live schedule, and a weekly walk-through with Jordan. Variations are priced and approved before work happens, never after.

05

Handover and beyond

A full defects walk, all certificates and manuals, and the statutory builder's warranty. We answer the phone after handover, which is not universal in this industry.

Do I need an architect before contacting you?

Can you build from plans I already have?

Yes. We'll review the documentation, flag anything that will be expensive or difficult to build, and cost it line by line before you commit.

Design and approvals typically run longer than people expect, and construction depends on scale and site. We give you a stage-by-stage programme before you sign, and update it monthly.

The best extensions look like the house always intended to go that way.

Most of our extension clients love where they live and have run out of room in it. The land is right, the street is right, and moving would mean buying back a worse version of what they already have.

The craft is in the join — where new structure meets a hundred-year-old wall, where the roofline changes, where the old floor level doesn't quite match the new. That junction is where extensions succeed or look like an afterthought.

How it runs

From first conversation
to handover.

01

Feasibility on your site

Before anything is drawn, we look at what your title, your council and your existing structure will actually allow. Heritage overlays, boundary setbacks and easements decide a lot.

02

Design that respects the original

Whether the answer is a sympathetic continuation or a deliberate contrast, the decision should be made on purpose. We work through it with you and your designer.

03

Investigation before pricing

We open up walls, check footings and confirm what's behind the plaster before we price it. Guessing here is how extensions blow out.

04

Open-book costing

You see the full schedule, including allowances for the unknowns that old houses hide. Contingency is named, not buried.

05

Living through it

Where possible we stage the work so you can stay in the house. Dust barriers, sequenced services and a site that gets swept at the end of every day.

Can we live in the house during the extension?

Often yes, depending on scope and whether kitchen or bathroom services are affected. We'll tell you honestly at feasibility stage, including the weeks that will be genuinely unpleasant.

How do you handle heritage overlays?

We deal with Adelaide councils regularly and know where they hold firm. Getting the front elevation and materials right early avoids a costly round of amended plans.

What if you find something unexpected in the old structure?

It happens with older homes — footings, termite history, asbestos, previous unpermitted work. Because we investigate before pricing and carry named allowances, discoveries change the schedule rather than blindsiding the budget.

Do you do second storeys on older homes?

Yes, subject to the existing footings and structure. That assessment is part of feasibility, and we'd rather tell you it isn't viable than find out halfway up.

Adelaide has some of the best housing stock in the country. Most of it was built for a life nobody lives any more.

A whole-home renovation is the hardest work we do. You're threading new services through solid stone, correcting a century of settlement, and doing it without losing the reason you bought the house.

We sequence it structure-first: footings, framing, waterproofing and services all resolved before a single finish is chosen. It's the least glamorous order of operations and the only one that lasts.

How it runs

From first conversation
to handover.

01

Condition assessment

A proper look at what you've bought: footings, damp, roof structure, wiring, previous work. You get a written picture before you commit to a scope.

02

Scope and priorities

We help you separate what must be done from what you want done, and what can wait for a second stage without wasting money.

03

Structure and services first

Underpinning, damp treatment, re-roofing, rewiring and plumbing. Unglamorous, expensive, and the reason the finishes stay looking good.

04

Joinery and finishes

Kitchens, sculleries, bathrooms and built-in joinery, made to suit the proportions of the original rooms rather than fighting them.

05

Reconciliation and handover

Every provisional sum reconciled against real invoices, shown to you, with the balance returned rather than absorbed.

Common questions

Should we renovate or knock down and rebuild?

Sometimes rebuilding is the honest answer, and we'll say so. It usually comes down to the condition of the existing structure, what the planning overlay allows and how much of the original you actually want to keep.

Can a renovation be staged?

Yes, and for many homes it should be. We plan stage one so it doesn't have to be undone later — services roughed in, structure resolved, so stage two is finishes rather than demolition.

How do you deal with damp in bluestone and stone homes?

Rising damp is common in Adelaide's older stone housing. The fix depends on the cause — ground levels, failed damp course, sealed render trapping moisture — so we diagnose before quoting a treatment.

Will the renovation match the original detailing?

Where you want it to. We can match cornices, skirtings and joinery profiles, or draw a clear line between old and new. Both work; the mistake is doing it accidentally.

What you receive

Four documents,

01

The costing schedule

Line by line, trade by trade. Every item carries the quote or rate behind it, so you can see what a number is made of rather than taking it on faith.

02

Named allowances

Where something genuinely can't be priced yet, it's shown as a provisional sum with the assumption written next to it — not folded quietly into a larger figure.

Our margin

Stated as its own line. You know what we're making on your house, which means you never have to wonder whether it's buried somewhere else.

Monthly reconciliation

As real invoices land, allowances are reconciled against them and the schedule is reissued. Savings go back to you rather than being absorbed.

Common questions

Things people ask
before they commit.

Doesn't showing your margin invite clients to negotiate it down?

Occasionally. More often it ends the conversation about margin altogether, because you can see it's reasonable and you stop wondering what's hidden in the other numbers.

What is a provisional sum, and why does it matter?

It's an allowance for work that can't be priced exactly yet — often because a selection hasn't been made or something is still hidden. Under an open book, every provisional sum is reconciled against the real invoice and the difference goes back to you.

How is this different from a fixed-price contract?

It isn't an alternative to one. You can still have a fixed price. The difference is that you can see the schedule that produced it, so you know which parts are firm and which carry allowances.

Do other Adelaide builders do this?

Some do parts of it. Showing the margin line itself is rarer, and it's the line that matters, because it's the one clients assume is being padded.

About

Four generations, one city.

Templeton Built is a family building company in Thebarton. Jordan is the fourth generation of his family to build in Adelaide, and the work still carries the family name for a reason.

[/et_pb_code][/et_pb_column][/et_pb_row][/et_pb_section][et_pb_section fb_built="1" _builder_version="4.27.0" custom_padding="0px||0px||true|false"][et_pb_row _builder_version="4.27.0" width="100%" max_width="100%" custom_padding="0px||0px||true|false"][et_pb_column type="4_4" _builder_version="4.27.0"][et_pb_code _builder_version="4.27.0"]

Jordan's great-grandfather, Peter Wyten, was raising sheds across Adelaide with his sons. That's where this starts.

The business Jordan runs today began as a property development company founded by his father. Jordan completed a carpentry apprenticeship, worked every part of the business from the tools through to project management, and gradually turned it toward what it is now: a builder of custom homes, extensions and renovations across metropolitan Adelaide and the Hills.

Why the company is deliberately small

We take on a limited number of projects each year. That isn't modesty — it's the only structure in which Jordan can genuinely be on every site. A larger operation would mean handing your build to a project manager you met once at contract signing.

It also means we're selective, and occasionally we'll tell you we're not the right builder for a project. That's a better outcome for everyone than taking work we can't give proper attention.

What we're actually good at

Old houses. Adelaide's stone villas, bungalows and character homes behave differently to new construction, and the difference between a builder who's worked on a hundred of them and one who hasn't shows up in the first fortnight.

Complicated sites. Fall, access, heritage overlays, neighbours, soil. The constraints that make architects interested tend to be the ones that make builders nervous.

Telling you the truth about money. Which is what the open book is for.

We'd rather lose a job at the quoting stage than lose your trust at the framing stage.

The brief

The owners had lived in the house for several years and knew exactly what didn't work: a kitchen tucked into the darkest corner of the plan, bedrooms that opened off each other, and a rear addition from the 1980s that turned its back on the garden.

What we found

Behind the plaster, two earlier renovations had left services running in places nobody would design them, and structural work that had never been certified. Before we could talk about finishes, that had to be corrected and documented.

The work

We removed the later addition entirely, corrected and underpinned where the structure required it, and rebuilt the rear of the house to open to the north. Original rooms at the front were restored rather than reinvented — cornices, joinery profiles and fireplaces retained and repaired.

The result

The front of the house reads as it always did from the street. The back is unmistakably contemporary, and every room now gets light for some part of the day.

Coastal exposure changes the specification. Fixings, flashings, glazing and external finishes all have to be selected for salt air, and the difference between doing that properly and not shows up within five years.

A rear addition with a covered alfresco that works as a genuine second living room rather than a paved afterthought. Sightlines were set so the kitchen bench looks straight down the yard.

Costing

What actually sets your build budget

Floor area is the number everyone fixates on. It's rarely the one doing the damage.

[/et_pb_code][/et_pb_column][/et_pb_row][/et_pb_section][et_pb_section fb_built="1" _builder_version="4.27.0" custom_padding="0px||0px||true|false"][et_pb_row _builder_version="4.27.0" width="100%" max_width="100%" custom_padding="0px||0px||true|false"][et_pb_column type="4_4" _builder_version="4.27.0"][et_pb_code _builder_version="4.27.0"]

Area is a poor proxy for cost

Two homes of identical size on two different Adelaide sites can differ enormously in cost. The variables that move the number hardest are the ones you can't see on a floor plan: soil classification, fall across the site, access for machinery, and how far services have to travel.

Site works are the quiet line item

Retaining, excavation, drainage and driveway access on a sloping block can consume a meaningful share of a budget before a single wall is framed. On flat sand in the western suburbs, the same house costs materially less to get out of the ground.

Specification compounds

A single decision — say, moving from standard aluminium windows to thermally broken commercial glazing — doesn't just cost more per unit. It changes the framing, the flashing details and sometimes the structure. The good news is the reverse is also true: one or two well-chosen downgrades can fund something you care about more.

What to do about it

Get a builder to look at your site before the design is finalised. It is the cheapest hour in the entire process and it routinely saves a redesign.

Renovate or knock down and rebuild?

The honest answer depends on four things, and sentiment is only one of them.

[/et_pb_code][/et_pb_column][/et_pb_row][/et_pb_section][et_pb_section fb_built="1" _builder_version="4.27.0" custom_padding="0px||0px||true|false"][et_pb_row _builder_version="4.27.0" width="100%" max_width="100%" custom_padding="0px||0px||true|false"][et_pb_column type="4_4" _builder_version="4.27.0"][et_pb_code _builder_version="4.27.0"]

What condition is the existing structure in?

Footings, roof structure, damp history and previous unpermitted work all matter more than the appearance of the house. A beautiful home sitting on failing footings can be more expensive to save than to replace.

What does the planning overlay allow?

In parts of Adelaide, demolition simply isn't on the table, or a rebuild would come with constraints tighter than what you already have. This is the first thing to check, not the last.

How much of the original do you actually want?

Some people want the rooms; others want the facade and nothing behind it. Being honest about this early prevents paying to retain things you don't value.

What is the street worth?

In established suburbs, the character of the existing home is part of the value. In others, it isn't. That calculation is different in Hawthorn than it is on a new subdivision.

Decide honestly whether you can

The question isn't whether it's possible — it usually is. It's whether you can tolerate six to nine months of it. Households with small children, shift workers and anyone working from home should think hard.

The services are the pinch point

You can live without a formal living room for a long time. You cannot live without a functioning bathroom or a way to cook. Good staging protects those two things for as long as possible and compresses the gap when it comes.

Set the site rules up front

Start times, access routes, where trades park, whether the dog can be in the yard. Agreeing this in week one prevents most of the friction that builds over a long job.

Budget for a fortnight away

There is almost always a two-week window that is genuinely miserable. Planning to be elsewhere for it is money well spent.
